title: Photosynthesis
passage: Photosynthesis is the process by which green plants make their own food. Using sunlight, water, and carbon dioxide, plants produce glucose and release oxygen. This process takes place mainly in the leaves. Chlorophyll, the green pigment in leaves, absorbs sunlight. Without photosynthesis, life on Earth would not be possible because plants form the base of most food chains and produce the oxygen that animals need to breathe.

questions.question: What is the main idea of the passage?
options: Photosynthesis is how plants make food and oxygen.
Only water is needed for plant growth.
questions.explanation: The passage explains photosynthesis as the process plants use to make food and oxygen.

questions.question: Where does photosynthesis mainly take place?
questions.explanation: The passage states it takes place mainly in the leaves.

questions.question: The word "release" in the passage is closest in meaning to:
questions.explanation: Release means to let out or set free.

title: The Printing Press
passage: The invention of the printing press in the 15th century changed the world. Before its invention, books were copied by hand, which made them expensive and rare. Johannes Gutenberg developed a system using movable type that allowed books to be produced more quickly and cheaply. As a result, knowledge spread more widely across Europe. Literacy rates increased, and new ideas in science, religion, and politics reached more people. Historians often consider the printing press one of the most important inventions in human history.

questions.question: What is the main idea of the passage?
options: The printing press greatly increased the spread of knowledge.
Literacy decreased after the printing press.
questions.explanation: The passage focuses on how the printing press spread knowledge.

questions.question: How were books produced before the printing press?
questions.explanation: Books were copied by hand.

questions.question: What can be inferred about books after the printing press was invented?
options: They became more available to ordinary people.
questions.explanation: Cheaper and faster production meant wider availability.

questions.question: The word "rare" in the passage is closest in meaning to:
questions.explanation: Rare means uncommon or not found often.

title: Sleep and Memory
passage: Sleep plays an essential role in memory and learning. During sleep, the brain processes information from the day and strengthens important memories. Studies show that students who sleep well before an exam often perform better than those who stay awake all night. Sleep also helps the brain clear waste products that build up during waking hours. Experts recommend seven to nine hours of sleep per night for most adults. Poor sleep can affect concentration, mood, and long-term health.

questions.question: What is the main idea of the passage?
options: Sleep supports memory, learning, and health.
Adults need only three hours of sleep.
questions.explanation: The passage explains the benefits of sleep for memory and health.

questions.question: How many hours of sleep do experts recommend for most adults?
questions.explanation: Experts recommend seven to nine hours.

questions.question: The word "strengthens" in the passage is closest in meaning to:
questions.explanation: Strengthens means makes stronger.

title: Renewable Energy
passage: Renewable energy comes from sources that are naturally replenished, such as sunlight, wind, and water. Unlike fossil fuels, renewable energy produces little or no greenhouse gas emissions during operation. Many countries are investing in solar panels and wind turbines to reduce dependence on coal and oil. Although the initial cost of renewable systems can be high, prices have fallen significantly in recent years. Challenges remain, including energy storage and the need for infrastructure upgrades. Still, renewable energy is widely seen as a key solution to climate change.

questions.question: What is the main idea of the passage?
options: Fossil fuels are the only option.
Renewable energy offers environmental benefits despite some challenges.
questions.explanation: The passage presents benefits and challenges of renewable energy.

questions.question: What is one challenge of renewable energy mentioned?
questions.explanation: Energy storage is listed as a challenge.

questions.question: The word "replenished" in the passage is closest in meaning to:
questions.explanation: Replenished means refilled or restored.

title: The Importance of Reading
passage: Reading is one of the most valuable skills a person can develop. It improves vocabulary, strengthens concentration, and expands knowledge about the world. People who read regularly tend to have better writing skills and stronger critical thinking abilities. Reading also reduces stress and can improve mental health. Experts recommend reading for at least twenty minutes every day. Whether it is books, newspapers, or online articles, any form of reading can bring benefits. For students preparing for exams like the TOEFL, regular reading practice is especially important because it builds the language skills needed for success.

questions.question: What is the main idea of the passage?
options: Reading is only useful for students.
questions.explanation: The passage focuses on the many benefits of reading.

questions.question: According to the passage, how long should people read each day?
questions.explanation: Experts recommend at least twenty minutes every day.

questions.question: The word "expands" in the passage is closest in meaning to:
questions.explanation: Expands means increases or makes larger.

title: Online Learning
passage: Online learning has become increasingly popular in recent years. Students can attend classes from anywhere with an internet connection, which provides great flexibility. Many working adults appreciate the ability to study while keeping their jobs. However, online learning also has challenges. Some students struggle with motivation and time management when there is no physical classroom. Technical problems can interrupt lessons. Despite these difficulties, research shows that online courses can be just as effective as traditional classes when students are motivated and the materials are well designed. Universities around the world continue to expand their online programs.

questions.question: What is the main idea of the passage?
options: Online learning is always better than traditional classes.
Online learning has both advantages and challenges.
Only working adults use online learning.
Technical problems make online learning impossible.
questions.explanation: The passage discusses both benefits and challenges.

questions.question: According to the passage, what do some students struggle with in online learning?
questions.explanation: Some students struggle with motivation and time management.

questions.question: What can be inferred about online courses?
options: They can be effective if students are motivated and materials are good.
They are only for young students.
questions.explanation: Research shows they can be effective under the right conditions.

questions.question: The word "flexibility" in the passage is closest in meaning to:
questions.explanation: Flexibility means the ability to change or adapt easily.

title: The Role of Teachers
passage: Teachers play a central role in education. They do more than just present information; they also inspire students, guide them through difficulties, and help them develop critical thinking skills. A good teacher can make a subject interesting even if students initially find it boring. Research shows that the quality of teaching has a strong effect on student achievement. In addition to subject knowledge, effective teachers need strong communication skills and patience. Many countries are working to improve teacher training programs because they recognize how important teachers are to the future of society.

questions.question: What is the main idea of the passage?
options: Teachers play an important role in education and student success.
questions.explanation: The passage emphasizes the important role of teachers.

questions.question: According to the passage, what do effective teachers need besides subject knowledge?
questions.explanation: Effective teachers need strong communication skills and patience.

questions.question: The word "inspire" in the passage is closest in meaning to:
questions.explanation: Inspire means to motivate or encourage.

title: Time Management for Students
passage: Many students struggle with time management. Between classes, homework, and other activities, it can be hard to finish everything on time. Experts suggest making a weekly schedule and setting clear priorities. Breaking large tasks into smaller steps also helps reduce stress. Avoiding distractions such as social media during study time can significantly improve focus. Students who manage their time well usually perform better academically and feel less anxious. Developing good time management habits early is one of the most useful skills for both school and future work.

questions.question: What is the main idea of the passage?
options: Students should never use social media.
Time management is important and can be improved with good habits.
Homework is the biggest problem for students.
Only experts can manage time well.
questions.explanation: The passage focuses on the importance of time management and practical tips.

questions.question: According to the passage, what can help reduce stress?
options: Breaking large tasks into smaller steps
questions.explanation: Breaking large tasks into smaller steps helps reduce stress.

questions.question: The word "distractions" in the passage is closest in meaning to:
questions.explanation: Distractions are things that take attention away.

title: The Benefits of Learning a Second Language
passage: Learning a second language offers many advantages beyond communication. Research shows that bilingual people often have better memory and problem-solving skills. Learning another language can also improve understanding of one's own language. In a globalized world, knowing more than one language increases job opportunities and cultural awareness. Although learning a language takes time and effort, the long-term benefits make it worthwhile. Many experts recommend starting as early as possible, but adults can also achieve high levels of proficiency with consistent practice.

questions.question: What is the main idea of the passage?
options: Only children can learn a second language.
Learning a second language has many cognitive and practical benefits.
Language learning is not useful for jobs.
questions.explanation: The passage discusses various benefits of learning a second language.

questions.question: According to the passage, what do bilingual people often have?
questions.explanation: Research shows bilingual people often have better memory and problem-solving skills.

questions.question: What can be inferred about adult language learners?
options: They can succeed with consistent practice.
questions.explanation: Adults can achieve high proficiency with consistent practice.

questions.question: The word "proficiency" in the passage is closest in meaning to:
questions.explanation: Proficiency means a high degree of skill or ability.

title: Cognitive Load and Learning
passage: Cognitive load theory suggests that working memory has limited capacity, and instructional design should therefore avoid overloading learners. Intrinsic cognitive load is determined by the inherent difficulty of the material and the learner's prior knowledge. Extraneous load results from poorly designed materials that force learners to process unnecessary information. Germane load refers to the mental effort devoted to schema construction and automation. Effective teaching minimizes extraneous load while managing intrinsic load and promoting germane processing. Strategies such as worked examples, segmented instruction, and dual-channel presentation of information have been shown to improve learning outcomes, particularly for complex academic content of the kind tested on standardized examinations.

questions.question: What is the main idea of the passage?
options: Instructional design should manage cognitive load to improve learning.
Only prior knowledge matters in learning.
questions.explanation: The passage centers on managing cognitive load through good instructional design.

questions.question: According to the passage, what causes extraneous cognitive load?
questions.explanation: Extraneous load results from poorly designed materials.

questions.question: What can be inferred about worked examples?
options: They can help manage cognitive load and improve learning.
They are only useful for simple content.
They replace the need for prior knowledge.
questions.explanation: Worked examples are listed as strategies that improve learning outcomes.

questions.question: The word "inherent" in the passage is closest in meaning to:
options: existing as a natural part of something
questions.explanation: Inherent means existing as a permanent or essential characteristic.

questions.question: Germane load is associated with:
questions.explanation: Germane load is mental effort devoted to schema construction and automation.

title: Urbanization and Sustainability
passage: Rapid urbanization presents both opportunities and challenges for sustainable development. Cities concentrate economic activity, innovation, and cultural exchange, yet they also generate significant environmental pressure through energy consumption, waste production, and habitat loss. Sustainable urban planning seeks to balance growth with environmental protection by promoting public transportation, green spaces, and energy-efficient buildings. Research indicates that compact city designs can reduce per capita emissions compared with sprawling suburban patterns. However, implementing such policies requires coordination among governments, businesses, and communities, as well as long-term investment. Without careful management, urbanization may intensify inequality and environmental degradation rather than improve quality of life.

questions.question: What is the main idea of the passage?
options: Urbanization has benefits and risks that require careful sustainable planning.
Only governments can solve urban problems.
questions.explanation: The passage discusses both sides of urbanization and the need for sustainable planning.

questions.question: According to the passage, compact city designs can:
options: Reduce per capita emissions compared with sprawling patterns
questions.explanation: Research indicates compact designs can reduce per capita emissions.

questions.question: What can be inferred if urbanization is not carefully managed?
options: Quality of life will automatically improve.
Inequality and environmental problems may worsen.
questions.explanation: Without careful management, inequality and degradation may intensify.

questions.question: The word "intensify" in the passage is closest in meaning to:
questions.explanation: Intensify means to become or make more intense.

title: Epistemic Uncertainty in Policy Modelling
passage: Contemporary policy analysis increasingly distinguishes between aleatory uncertainty, which arises from inherent randomness in the systems under study, and epistemic uncertainty, which stems from incomplete knowledge, model misspecification, or contested theoretical assumptions. While probabilistic methods are reasonably well adapted to the former, the latter often requires qualitatively different tools: sensitivity analysis, scenario planning, and structured expert elicitation. A recurring difficulty is that decision-makers tend to treat model outputs as more authoritative than the underlying assumptions warrant, particularly when results are presented with numerical precision. Scholars of science and technology studies have therefore argued for greater transparency regarding the pedigree of evidence and for institutional mechanisms that prevent the premature closure of debate. In high-stakes domains such as climate adaptation and financial regulation, failing to maintain this distinction can produce policies that are brittle precisely where flexibility is most needed.

questions.question: What is the central claim of the passage?
options: All uncertainty in policy models is random and can be handled with probability alone.
Distinguishing epistemic from aleatory uncertainty is essential, and treating model outputs as definitive can produce brittle policy.
Expert elicitation should replace quantitative modelling entirely.
Numerical precision always improves decision quality.
questions.explanation: The passage argues for distinguishing uncertainty types and warns against over-authoritative use of model outputs.

questions.question: According to the passage, epistemic uncertainty arises from:
options: Incomplete knowledge, misspecification, or contested assumptions
questions.explanation: Epistemic uncertainty stems from incomplete knowledge, model misspecification, or contested assumptions.

questions.question: What can be inferred about presenting results with numerical precision?
options: It always clarifies uncertainty for decision-makers.
It may encourage decision-makers to overestimate the authority of model outputs.
It eliminates the need for sensitivity analysis.
It is irrelevant to policy debate.
questions.explanation: The passage notes decision-makers treat precise outputs as more authoritative than assumptions warrant.

questions.question: The word "brittle" in the passage is closest in meaning to:
options: fragile or easily broken under stress
questions.explanation: Brittle here means fragile — policies that break when conditions change.

questions.question: Which tools does the passage associate with managing epistemic uncertainty?
options: Sensitivity analysis, scenario planning, and structured expert elicitation
questions.explanation: Those three approaches are listed explicitly for epistemic uncertainty.

title: Institutional Path Dependence
passage: Path dependence denotes the process by which early, often contingent choices constrain later options, making reversal costly even when superior alternatives become available. In institutional economics, this concept helps explain why inefficient arrangements persist: sunk costs, network externalities, and complementary practices raise the price of switching. Classic illustrations include the persistence of the QWERTY keyboard layout and the continued use of particular legal doctrines long after their original rationale has eroded. Critics caution, however, that invoking path dependence can become a residual explanation that merely redescribes inertia without identifying mechanisms. More rigorous applications specify the feedback loops—cognitive, political, or technological—that reinforce the status quo and the critical junctures at which change remains feasible. For reformers, the implication is not fatalism but timing: interventions are most effective when complementary supports are weak or when external shocks temporarily lower switching costs.

questions.question: What is the main idea of the passage?
options: Path dependence means change is always impossible.
Path dependence explains persistent arrangements through early constraints and switching costs, but requires careful mechanistic analysis.
QWERTY is the only valid example of path dependence.
Reformers should never attempt institutional change.
questions.explanation: The passage defines path dependence, notes risks of vague use, and stresses mechanisms and timing for reform.

questions.question: According to the passage, what raises the cost of switching institutions?
options: Sunk costs, network externalities, and complementary practices
questions.explanation: These three factors are listed as raising switching costs.

questions.question: What do critics of path-dependence explanations warn against?
options: Using the concept as a residual label for inertia without specifying mechanisms
questions.explanation: Critics say it can become a residual explanation that redescribes inertia without mechanisms.

questions.question: The word "contingent" in the passage is closest in meaning to:
options: dependent on chance or particular circumstances
questions.explanation: Contingent here means dependent on particular, often accidental, circumstances.

title: Measurement Error and Attenuation Bias
passage: Classical measurement error in an explanatory variable biases ordinary least squares estimates toward zero—a phenomenon known as attenuation bias. When the variable of interest is measured with random noise uncorrelated with the true value and with the disturbance term, the estimated coefficient is a fraction of the true effect, with the degree of attenuation increasing in the noise-to-signal ratio. This result has far-reaching implications for empirical work: null findings may reflect poor measurement rather than the absence of an effect, and comparisons across studies become hazardous when measurement quality differs. Strategies to mitigate the problem include instrumental variables that isolate exogenous variation in the true signal, repeated measures that allow reliability ratios to be estimated, and structural models that incorporate the measurement process explicitly. None of these remedies is costless; each imposes additional assumptions whose plausibility must be defended. Consequently, careful discussion of measurement is not a technical afterthought but a substantive component of credible causal inference.

questions.question: What is the main idea of the passage?
options: Measurement error always inflates estimated effects.
Classical measurement error attenuates coefficients toward zero and requires careful remedial strategies whose assumptions must be justified.
Instrumental variables eliminate all forms of bias.
Null findings always mean there is no true effect.
questions.explanation: The passage explains attenuation bias and stresses careful, assumption-laden remedies.

questions.question: Under classical measurement error, the estimated coefficient is:
options: A fraction of the true effect, shrinking as noise rises relative to signal
questions.explanation: Attenuation increases with the noise-to-signal ratio.

questions.question: What can be inferred about null findings in the presence of measurement error?
options: They prove the theory is false.
They may reflect weak measurement rather than a true null effect.
questions.explanation: The passage notes null findings may reflect poor measurement rather than no effect.

questions.question: The word "plausibility" in the passage is closest in meaning to:
questions.explanation: Plausibility means how reasonable or credible something appears.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT listed as a strategy to address measurement error?
questions.explanation: Ignoring measurement is the opposite of what the passage recommends.

title: Legitimacy and Compliance
passage: Legal scholars and political scientists have long distinguished compliance driven by deterrence from compliance grounded in legitimacy—the belief that authorities have a rightful claim to obedience. Procedural justice research suggests that people are more willing to accept outcomes, even unfavourable ones, when they perceive decision-making as fair, transparent, and respectful. This insight complicates purely instrumental accounts of regulation: increasing sanctions may raise compliance in the short run yet erode the reservoir of voluntary cooperation on which complex regulatory systems depend. Empirical studies in tax administration, policing, and environmental enforcement find that perceived fairness often predicts compliance more strongly than expected penalties alone. The policy implication is not that deterrence is irrelevant, but that legitimacy is a strategic resource. Authorities that neglect procedural quality risk costly cycles of surveillance and punishment that deliver diminishing returns.

questions.question: What is the central argument of the passage?
options: Legitimacy based on fair procedure sustains compliance and complements deterrence; neglecting it is strategically costly.
questions.explanation: The passage argues legitimacy from procedural fairness supports compliance beyond deterrence alone.

questions.question: According to procedural justice research, people accept outcomes more readily when:
options: Decision-making is perceived as fair, transparent, and respectful
questions.explanation: Fair, transparent, respectful process increases acceptance.

questions.question: What risk does the passage associate with relying only on stronger sanctions?
options: Erosion of voluntary cooperation and diminishing returns from enforcement
questions.explanation: Heavy deterrence can erode voluntary cooperation and yield diminishing returns.

questions.question: The word "reservoir" in the passage is closest in meaning to:
questions.explanation: Reservoir here means a stored stock of voluntary cooperation.

title: External Validity and Transportability
passage: A causal estimate recovered in one population does not automatically apply to another. External validity concerns whether an effect estimated under particular conditions generalizes; transportability asks more precisely what additional assumptions allow an effect to be carried from a source to a target population. Differences in covariate distributions, in the prevalence of effect modifiers, or in the very mechanisms linking treatment to outcome can all undermine naive extrapolation. Recent work in causal graphical models formalizes these conditions and clarifies when statistical adjustment, reweighting, or structural knowledge can support transport. The practical message for applied researchers is sobering: internal validity is necessary but not sufficient for policy relevance. Studies that report effects without characterizing the populations and contexts to which they might extend leave decision-makers without the information required for responsible use.

questions.question: What is the main idea of the passage?
options: Causal estimates always generalize across populations.
Transporting causal effects requires explicit assumptions; internal validity alone does not guarantee policy relevance.
Graphical models make external validity unnecessary.
questions.explanation: The passage stresses assumptions for transportability and limits of internal validity alone.

questions.question: Which factors can undermine naive extrapolation of causal effects?
options: Differences in covariates, effect modifiers, or causal mechanisms
questions.explanation: Those three classes of differences are listed explicitly.

questions.question: What does the passage imply about studies that omit population and context detail?
options: They are ideal for policy use.
They leave decision-makers without information needed for responsible application.
They automatically transport to all settings.
questions.explanation: Without characterizing populations and contexts, responsible use is hindered.

questions.question: The word "naive" in the passage is closest in meaning to:
questions.explanation: Naive extrapolation means overly simple, uncritical generalization.
